card.hook: A whole river walks off a cliff and drops straight into the Mediterranean, and it's the first photo most visitors take. You can see why.
card.stand_here: Stand on the cliff-top main viewing terrace in Düden Parkı, on the side facing the sea. The falls lie to the south-west of you, so face that way and you'll see the water leaving the cliff edge from the side, with the sea right beside it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x or 1x to get the fall, the cliff and the sea all in one frame. Then try zoom 2x or more to pick out just the falling water (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and sit the horizon on one of the lines, because the slope of the cliff can tilt your picture.
card.best_time: A photo guide recommends sunset, when the light gives strong tones against the sea. The light on the coast changes quickly, so take a few shots at each zoom.
card.selfie_here: Use the Düden Park terrace on top of the cliff, with the falls beside you and the sea behind. Switch to the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the falling water over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back on the same terrace while you stand at the cliff-top side with the falls beside you, so they can frame you with the whole waterfall in view.
card.rules_and_safety: You're at the top of the cliff, so keep an eye on the edges. Personal photos are freely permitted, and the park is free, but check the official site for current hours.
card.challenge: Take the same shot at zoom 1x and zoom 2x, then pick a winner. Bonus points if the water is mid-leap off the cliff edge.
card.good_to_know: The Düden River drops 40 metres (131 ft) off the cliff into the Mediterranean. There's no walking route down to the base, so a head-on view is only possible from a boat. Don't mix this up with Upper Düden, a separate, fenced site elsewhere in the province.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the cliff-top main viewing terrace in Düden Parkı, on the side facing the sea. The falls lie to the south-west of you, so face that way and you'll see the water leaving the cliff edge from the side, with the sea right beside it.

card.hook: Most people head straight down to the pebbles, but the better view is above them. Climb up to the glass pyramid and the whole curve of Konyaaltı Beach opens out, with mountains behind it.
card.stand_here: Stand at Cam Piramit, in the park and viewing terrace around the glass pyramid. Konyaaltı Beach is to the south-west, so face that way and look out over the beach, the park and the coast running toward Lara.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in the park, the pyramid and the whole sweep of beach. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural view, then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the mountains or a stretch of coast.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the mountains, then drag the slider down a little to make the picture darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon. The light is softer and the mountains are clearer than in the middle of a summer day.
card.selfie_here: Try the Antalya Photo Frame on Konyaaltı Beach, where the mountains and beach sit behind you. Use the front camera and zoom 0.5x to fit in more of the scenery. For sunset, a guide recommends the western end of the Konyaaltı promenade, with the Taurus peaks on one side and the sea on the other.
card.ask_someone: On the Konyaaltı panoramic terrace, ask a passer-by to stand a few steps back and face you while you stand with the beach and mountains behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the public walkways, because swimming and beach-club areas may limit where you can stand on the sand. At the panoramic terrace, keep a close eye on small children near the railings.
card.challenge: Use the gridlines to put the horizon on the top or bottom line, then add the glass pyramid in the foreground. Bonus points if the mountains sit perfectly level.
card.good_to_know: Konyaaltı is one of Antalya's two main beaches, the other being Lara. It runs about 13 km along the western side of the city and holds Blue Flag status for water quality. The shore is mostly fine pebbles with some sand, and Turkish pines and hibiscus grow along the front.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Cam Piramit, in the park and viewing terrace around the glass pyramid. Konyaaltı Beach is to the south-west, so face that way and look out over the beach, the park and the coast running toward Lara.

card.hook: You're strolling along a busy boulevard, and suddenly there's a white marble Roman gate with three arches, sitting right between the modern city and the Old Town. It's only about 8 metres high, so it feels friendly and easy to fit in your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand on Atatürk Caddesi, on the boulevard side, facing the gate from the modern-city end. Line yourself up with the middle arch so the Old Town lanes open up behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get all three arches in. If the pavement is crowded and you can't step back, try zoom 0.5x, but keep the gate in the centre so the edges don't stretch. Then go to zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the lion heads and flower carvings.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line the pillars up with the vertical lines so the whole gate stands up straight.
card.best_time: One guide suggests the western side in the morning, with the sun behind you, but that's unconfirmed, so check the light when you arrive. If you're there after dark, try night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Step under the central arch and stand on the original marble paving stones, facing the Kaleiçi side. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x so the arch and carvings fit in around you. This is a framing suggestion rather than a classic spot, so play with it.
card.ask_someone: Ask your passer-by to stand on the Atatürk Boulevard side, a few steps back from the gate so the three arches and both towers fit in one frame, while you stand in front of the arches.
card.rules_and_safety: The gate sits on a busy boulevard, so wait for a gap in the traffic before you shoot. You can walk through it, but check the official site first if you plan to climb the tower or visit at a particular time.
card.challenge: Can you catch both eras in one frame? The southern tower is Roman, and the top of the northern tower was rebuilt in the 13th century and has an Arabic inscription.
card.good_to_know: Hadrian's Gate honours the emperor Hadrian, who visited the city in 130 CE. It's the only surviving entrance gate in the old city walls, and the walls hid it for years, which helped protect it. It was restored in 1959, and a clear panel in the central arch lets you look down at the original Roman paving, with deep cart grooves worn into it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Atatürk Caddesi, on the boulevard side, facing the gate from the modern-city end. Line yourself up with the middle arch so the Old Town lanes open up behind it.

card.hook: Picture the entrance with people drifting past, and you waiting a few seconds for a clear gap. That's the whole trick here: treat the aquarium like a landmark, get the big front-on shot first, then go hunting for details.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon on the map, which sits right at the aquarium itself. Face the entrance and outer walls from there, then step back if it's safe and you need more of the building in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the building and entrance. If you're close and the whole front won't fit, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for signs and details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go when it's quieter for a clearer view of the entrance. Soft light in the morning or later in the afternoon is kinder than harsh midday sun.
card.selfie_here: Go inside for the 131-metre underwater tunnel, where sharks and fish swim overhead and you get the aquarium's signature view behind you. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x if you want more of the scene, and keep the tunnel over your shoulder. There's also a green-screen photo area inside, so ask staff at the entrance or souvenir shop where to find it.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally fine inside, but don't use flash, especially near tanks. Photos and videos aren't allowed in some restricted areas, named as the shark tank and the VR 360 zone. Check the official site before you go for current rules and access.
card.challenge: Grab one wide shot of the whole entrance, then find one sign, colour or shape up close and make it look like a postcard.
card.good_to_know: The building works well as a landmark shot, so take one wide frame for the setting and one closer one for detail. Fire off a few quick shots in a row and keep the sharpest. The official site has the latest on access arrangements.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the phone icon on the map, which sits right at the aquarium itself. Face the entrance and outer walls from there, then step back if it's safe and you need more of the building in the frame.

card.hook: Here's an honest one: the Antalya Museum is closed, and you're visiting a building site where the galleries used to be. Demolition began in 2025 and a new building is being planned, so think of this as a quick stop and a 'I was here while it changed' photo.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, which marks the museum site itself, and face the plot to take in its long, low outline (or what's left of it). If fencing or works block the way, step back to the nearest open public spot and shoot from there, and don't go into any closed area.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole plot in, which is roughly 180 metres across. Then go to 1x for a natural view of the building or hoardings, and 2x or 5x (if your phone has them) for signs and details from a distance.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then slide the brightness a touch darker if the sky is bright so the walls don't turn gloomy.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows than midday. It may also be quieter outside working hours.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera from the nearest open public spot, with the site behind you over your shoulder, and try 0.5x so you fit more in. Older guides mention a Garden of Sculptures near the entrance, but with the site closed, don't count on getting in there.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by near the tram stop across Konyaaltı Caddesi, where the old tram's last stop was, to take your photo while you stand on the museum side of the road. That spot comes from an older guide, so check it on the ground first.
card.rules_and_safety: The site may be restricted and can change from week to week, so check the official site before you go. Stay out of any closed area.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole site, then find one sign or detail that tells the story and frame it so the city is still in the background.
card.good_to_know: Antalya Museum was one of Turkey's largest museums, with 13 exhibition halls, an open-air gallery and about 5,000 works from the Mediterranean coast and ancient Pamphylia. It was best known for its Roman statues from Perge, including Plancia Magna, and a hall of carved sarcophagi. It was also the first Turkish museum building to come out of an architectural competition, held in 1964.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, which marks the museum site itself, and face the plot to take in its long, low outline (or what's left of it). If fencing or works block the way, step back to the nearest open public spot and shoot from there, and don't go into any closed area.

card.hook: Picture an old tower on a cliff edge with the sea and the whole curve of Antalya's coastline spread out behind it. That's the shot here, and the tower comes with a Roman-era backstory, so you get a good story to go with the picture.
card.stand_here: Stand on the cliff edge beside Hıdırlık Tower (Hıdırlık Kulesi), with Karaalioğlu Park about 200 m to the south-east. Face the sea so the tower sits in front of you with the coastline opening out behind it. Use the tower as your landmark, not the compass.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the tower and the sweep of coastline together. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look. Try 2x or 5x to pick out boats or a stretch of cliff (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sea or sky, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water and the tower. Midday sun can flatten the colours and make the sea glare.
card.selfie_here: Head to the middle mirador, the central cliff viewing terrace, and stand about three metres back from the railing. It's the one terrace where the sea and the Beydağları Mountains fit in one frame, so use the front camera, try 0.5x, and let them sit over your shoulder. For a fun alternative, pose with the Don Quixote statue on the cliffs between the second and third terraces, next to the large Chinese tree.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone on the walkway running beside the central terrace to take your photo while you stand on the terrace, about three metres back from the railing.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep well back from the cliff edge, and hold your phone with both hands so the horizon stays level. We couldn't confirm access to the park or the tower's entry rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines and park the horizon on a line with the tower on a side line. Can you make it look as neat as a postcard?
card.good_to_know: Karaalioğlu Park is a clifftop park on Antalya's coast, with gardens, fountains and sea views. The tower has a Roman-era backstory. Once you've got the wide view, wander into the park for quieter garden scenes, like the Dancing Girls statue (Dans Eden Kızlar Heykeli).
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the cliff edge beside Hıdırlık Tower (Hıdırlık Kulesi), with Karaalioğlu Park about 200 m to the south-east. Face the sea so the tower sits in front of you with the coastline opening out behind it. Use the tower as your landmark, not the compass.

card.hook: Picture a round stone tower sitting on a square base, glowing like warm toast while the sea turns gold behind it. That's Hıdırlık Tower, and it makes your photos look good with almost no effort.
card.stand_here: Stand on the seaward edge of Karaalioğlu Park, next to the tower, where the cliff-top is open. The tower is to the south-west of you, with the sea and the coast behind it, so face south-west and step back far enough to fit the whole tower with its base.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the tower, sea and coast in one frame. Use 0.5x only if you're close and the whole tower won't fit, and 2x or higher (it depends on your phone) for a tighter shot of the stone against the water.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then make the picture a little darker if the sky or sea is very bright, so the stone keeps its warm colour.
card.best_time: Go around sunset, when the light bounces off the water and adds colour to the stone.
card.selfie_here: Try the small paved plaza right at the foot of the tower, facing west toward the sea, where the open view has the Beydağları mountains on the horizon. Use the front camera at 0.5x and tilt it so the tower sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to shoot from behind the low stone wall about 12 metres from you, or from the path about 15 metres west of the tower, while you face the sea with the tower behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed around the tower and its viewing platform, but follow any posted photo signs. Reports disagree on whether you can go inside, so check the official site first. The spiral staircase inside is narrow and steep, so it may not suit anyone with mobility problems or claustrophobia.
card.challenge: Get the tower standing perfectly straight with the horizon dead level, using gridlines, and then see if your travel buddy can spot the difference.
card.good_to_know: The tower is about 14 metres high and is believed to have been built by the Romans in the second century CE. Later it was a Byzantine military outpost, a fortification and a lighthouse, and the upper section still shows Seljuk and Ottoman repairs. The name Hıdırlık refers to a place where the spring festival Hıdırellez is celebrated.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the seaward edge of Karaalioğlu Park, next to the tower, where the cliff-top is open. The tower is to the south-west of you, with the sea and the coast behind it, so face south-west and step back far enough to fit the whole tower with its base.

card.hook: Surprise: the Antalya Clock Tower looks paler than the photos you've probably seen. Restoration and stone cleaning have lightened it up, so you're not imagining it.
card.stand_here: Cross Cumhuriyet Meydanı to the far side and walk back about 30 metres from the tower, then turn around and face it. From there the whole tower fits in, with the old city-wall silhouette and some old arcade arches at one edge.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the whole tower fits. If you're closer and it won't fit, switch to 0.5x. Try zoom 2x or higher to crop out cables or taxis.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean, and leave a little sky above the dome.
card.best_time: After dark, when the tower is lit up and really stands out. Daytime works too, but the square gets busy at peak times.
card.selfie_here: Try the popular square in the Kale Kapısı district, beside the old town. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the Clock Tower over your shoulder, and check the square's exact name on your map first.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Cumhuriyet Street or in one of the squares near the tower so they can fit the whole thing in, while you pose with the tower behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Wear comfortable footwear, because the streets of Kaleiçi can be slippery.
card.challenge: Get the whole tower in the frame with zero taxis and zero cables. A few steps left or right usually does it, and you'll feel very smug.
card.good_to_know: The tower is a tall, narrow stone landmark in Cumhuriyet Meydanı. Its dome has been restored and the stone cleaned, which is why it looks lighter now. It's lit up after dark, and Cumhuriyet Caddesi gives you a wider street-level view if the square is too crowded.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Cross Cumhuriyet Meydanı to the far side and walk back about 30 metres from the tower, then turn around and face it. From there the whole tower fits in, with the old city-wall silhouette and some old arcade arches at one edge.

card.hook: Picture a row of yachts sitting in glass-calm water, with old walls and cliffs behind them and red-tiled houses stacked up the slope like a layer cake. It's the ancient port of Antalya, and it looks great even on a small phone screen.
card.stand_here: Stand at Kaleiçi Old Harbour, about 31 m north of the harbour, and face south across the basin. That puts the boats in front of you and the walls and rooftops behind them.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the harbour and rooftops, then try 0.5x to fit in more sky and sea. Zoom 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out boats, masts or a stretch of wall.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, so your photo is mostly rooftops and water or mostly sky.
card.best_time: Go in the golden hour before sunset, when the sun drops over the water. From the western side of Hıdırlık Kulesi, the sunset light is especially good.
card.selfie_here: Try the glass-paneled balcony in Keçili Park, which overlooks the Kaleiçi port. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low so the harbour fills the space behind your shoulder. The top viewing deck of the glass elevator also gives a wide view down over the boats and water.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your wallet in a front pocket, as the usual tourist reminder applies in Kaleiçi. Hıdırlık Kulesi is a public open-air tower, but check the official site before you go in case access has changed.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot first, then step in and find a mast that lines up against a red roof.
card.good_to_know: Kaleiçi means "Inner Castle", and the district is enclosed by a double ring of walls. It still has around 3,000 traditional houses with red-tiled roofs, with narrow alleys running uphill from the water. A few traces of the ancient harbour breakwater survive, so it's more than just a pretty marina.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Kaleiçi Old Harbour, about 31 m north of the harbour, and face south across the basin. That puts the boats in front of you and the walls and rooftops behind them.

card.hook: One red brick tower, eight ridges, and about 38 metres of "yes, this is Antalya." The Yivli Minaret rises over the gateway to Kaleiçi, so it's hard to miss and easy to love.
card.stand_here: Stand in Cumhuriyet Meydanı, on the south side of the square at the entrance to Kaleiçi. Face the minaret rising above the old-town entrance, and step back until you can fit the base and the top in one shot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole tower with some of the square. Then try 2x or 5x (if your phone goes that far) for the brick flutes and the traces of turquoise and dark blue tile near the top.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brick, not the sky, then slide to darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the square is quieter and cooler than at midday. Late-afternoon side light also looks great on the brick.
card.selfie_here: Head to the stone base of the minaret in the mosque grounds, where the square stonework meets the fluted brick shaft. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, hold it low, and let the tower rise over your shoulder. Check the backdrop on site before you tap.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by, stand in Cumhuriyet Meydanı with the minaret rising above the old-town entrance behind you, and ask them to step back far enough to catch the whole tower with some square at your feet.
card.rules_and_safety: The mosque is still used for worship, so be quiet and considerate. Photography is generally fine outside prayer times, but don't photograph worshippers or inside the prayer hall during prayer. Take your shoes off before stepping onto the carpeted prayer areas. One guide calls the area very safe and welcoming.
card.challenge: Play 'spot the leftover tile': zoom in and find a patch of the old turquoise or dark blue still clinging to the brick.
card.good_to_know: The first mosque here dates to around 1230, after the Seljuk takeover of the city, and it was rebuilt in 1373. Its prayer hall now has six domes. Restoration finished in 2010 and uncovered old water channels, which you can see through a glass section of floor.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Cumhuriyet Meydanı, on the south side of the square at the entrance to Kaleiçi. Face the minaret rising above the old-town entrance, and step back until you can fit the base and the top in one shot.

card.hook: This mosque doesn't show off. It has one big calm dome, one slender minaret, and a solid shape that practically poses for you.
card.stand_here: Head about 600 m north-west to Murat Pasha Mosque and stand in the forecourt at the front, facing the building. Use the map and your own eye to find the spot where the dome, its ten-sided drum and the minaret all fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the straight-on shot. If the forecourt is too tight to fit the whole building, try 0.5x. For the porch or the top of the minaret, use 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the minaret up with a vertical line so it stands straight, and leave a little sky above the dome.
card.best_time: Avoid prayer times. The mosque is calmer then, and you won't be pointing your phone at worshippers.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and try 0.5x so more of the building squeezes in. Turn so the dome and minaret sit over your shoulder, and hold the phone a little higher than your face.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working place of worship, so dress modestly (a head covering is recommended for women) and keep quiet. Don't use flash, and don't photograph people who are praying.
card.challenge: Zoom in on the porch and count the three domes sitting on pointed arches of coloured stone, held up by four round columns.
card.good_to_know: Murat Pasha of Karaman commissioned this Ottoman mosque in 1570. It's in the Muratpaşa district of Antalya. If you visit as a guest, look for the bands of calligraphy around the walls inside and the marble pulpit with its carved reliefs.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head about 600 m north-west to Murat Pasha Mosque and stand in the forecourt at the front, facing the building. Use the map and your own eye to find the spot where the dome, its ten-sided drum and the minaret all fit in one frame.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the Murat Pasha Mosque behind the visitor, or a spot where a passer-by should shoot the visitor with the whole mosque in frame, so I have left both fields empty rather than guess. The results were mostly general mosque listings and Kaleiçi photo guides. The Tripadvisor listing gives the address as Sarampol Avenue, and Wanderlog describes the courtyard with its orange tree and ceramics, but neither says where to stand for a photo. Several Pic2Map entries are Kaleiçi streets near the mosque, but they are unverified camera locations with no link to the mosque. The Republic Square and Hadrian's Gate tips in the Pretty Big Butterflies guide are real Kaleiçi viewpoints, but that page does not tie them to this mosque, so I excluded them. Photo etiquette is the only conduct advice found, and it is not a selfie-stick or tripod rule, so 'rules' is empty. Pages say to avoid taking many photos out of respect while people are praying, to avoid prayer times, and to avoid photographing people without consent; they also say women should cover their hair. Please check the coordinates you gave against the mosque's location on a map before using this in the app.

card.hook: The "Cut Minaret" doesn't look cut any more. Its cone and balcony were restored around 2019, so if you've seen older photos online, the real thing is a pleasant surprise.
card.stand_here: Stand on Hesapçı Sokak, on the stretch between Hadrian's Gate and the mosque, and look toward the minaret. It's to the east, at the far end of a narrow lane with old Kaleiçi houses on both sides.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so you get the lane and the houses leading to the minaret. If the lane feels too tight, tap 0.5x. Try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to bring the tower closer without stepping into the road.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the minaret on a vertical line, and let the house walls frame it on both sides.
card.best_time: Weekday mornings tend to be quieter, which really helps in such a narrow lane. Visit outside prayer times too.
card.selfie_here: Try the corner where Hesapçı Sokak meets Cami Sokak, where the minaret rises above the rooftops. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x if you want more in, and keep the minaret over your shoulder. Check the framing on the spot, as this is a good place to try rather than a marked photo stop.
card.rules_and_safety: The mosque is in use and the ruins around it are fenced off, so take your photos from the lane, not from inside the site. Be respectful, especially if people are going in or out.
card.challenge: Get the lane shot with the minaret on a grid line, the walls framing it, and not a single stranger in the picture. Patience wins here.
card.good_to_know: Kesik Minare is a mosque in Antalya's Kaleiçi old town, with a fenced ruin beside the minaret. The minaret's cone and balcony were restored around 2019, and the mosque reopened in 2021. For a second angle, walk to Cami Sokak and shoot from the corner, where the minaret rises straight above the ruin and the rooftops.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Hesapçı Sokak, on the stretch between Hadrian's Gate and the mosque, and look toward the minaret. It's to the east, at the far end of a narrow lane with old Kaleiçi houses on both sides.

selfie_research.notes: Weak evidence: no page I found names a specific selfie spot or a specific spot for a photographer to frame the whole minaret. The corner above is a location, not a stated photo spot, so check it on the ground. A Tripadvisor reviewer says 'a quick selfie from the outside is all you need' but names no spot. Airial mentions 'narrow streets leading to it' and 'higher vantage points in Kaleiçi' without naming them. Ask-someone spot left null for the same reason. No pages mention selfie stick or tripod rules. Access is uncertain: Tripadvisor lists the site as closed, a 2026 review describes a working mosque, Lonely Planet says the ruins are fenced off, and Turkey's For Life says the restored mosque opens at certain times. Fire dates also vary by source (1800, 1846, 1890, 1895).

card.hook: Count the domes and you'll lose track in a good way: one big one rising on a high rim, with three smaller ones lined up along the north side. It's a very clear shape, so even a quick snap looks good.
card.stand_here: Walk to the north side of Tekeli Mehmet Pasha Mosque and stand about 20 m north of its centre. Face the northern façade, so the main dome rises behind the northern domes.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the head-on view. If you can't step back far enough to fit all the domes in, switch to zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the tiled panels and window arches.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the façade level, then tap the façade and slide it a bit darker if the sky is bright so the dome keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the façade is evenly lit and keep the sun behind you. Early morning or late afternoon is usually quieter and kinder to the stonework.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the Clock Tower (Saat Kulesi) on Kaleiçi Square, where the mosque is immediately behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to squeeze more in, and let the mosque sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by in the mosque's forecourt, directly behind the Clock Tower, to take your photo while you stand with the front of the mosque behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working place of worship. Photos inside are fine without flash, but never during prayer. Be respectful of worshippers, and check locally for restoration work, because scaffolding can spoil the view.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole group of domes, then one close-up of a tiled panel. Can you tell the two apart at a glance?
card.good_to_know: Tekeli Mehmet Pasha Mosque is a 17th-century Ottoman mosque in Antalya's Kalekapisi district. It takes its name from Lala Mehmed Pasa. The main dome is held by three semi-domes to the east, west and south, and the pointed window arches carry tiled panels with Koranic verses in taliq script.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the north side of Tekeli Mehmet Pasha Mosque and stand about 20 m north of its centre. Face the northern façade, so the main dome rises behind the northern domes.
